cards.headline: One synth, one EP, and 2012's tune of the year
cards.snippet: Todd Terje built 'Inspector Norse' on a single machine. His fourth EP, It's the Arps, was recorded using only the ARP 2600 synthesizer, and this track — his debut single, released 19 June 2012 — became its calling card: Mixmag named it the top tune of 2012 and Resident Advisor placed it second on its year-end list. Two years later it closed his debut album, It's Album Time (2014), a record critics treated as the moment Norwegian space-disco stepped fully into the light.
cards.context: Terje — Terje Olsen — had spent years as a remixer and re-editor, and was called the 'king of the summer jams' by Mixmag.

cards.headline: The dancing man who gave the track its face
cards.snippet: The same day the single appeared, Pitchfork posted its official video: four minutes of a Norwegian man dancing alone — in his kitchen, on a bus, in the street — utterly unbothered. The man is Marius Solem Johansen, who had been posting his own ecstatic dance videos online under the alias 'Inspector Norse'. For most of the world the clip, not a club, is where this track lives, and its comment threads still fill with people standing up mid-listen to dance along in empty rooms.
cards.context: In the Pitchfork thread, viewers still argue over the excerpt's tone — pure joy, or despair with music as the only outlet.

cards.headline: The pact: 'we are not allowed to stop dancing until it's over'
cards.snippet: Over the years my friends and I have made a pact that if this song comes on at a party or club, we are not allowed to stop dancing until it's over. That has been a really fun pact. One time my girlfriend said "If you don't stop playing Inspector Norse I'll leave". I'll miss her
cards.context: The replies refuse to mourn the trade — 'i miss her too...............' and 'LOL never stop being you man!'.

replies.author: @Yungtacosss
replies.text: LOL never stop being you man!

cards.headline: 'This should be our planets official anthem'
cards.snippet: This should be our planets official anthem
cards.context: Most of its 45 replies are addressed to the commenter by name and so don't display; the one that stands alone answers, 'I don't think we deserve such a sweet anthem.'

replies.author: @tylerjones7433
replies.text: I don't think we deserve such a sweet anthem

cards.headline: For David, who had 'the most amazing moves to this song'
cards.snippet: A friend of mine who died nearly three years ago, had the most amazing moves to this song, I will never forget seeing him, smiling, shaking his hips, pointing fingers, wobbling his knees. Miss you so much David.
cards.context: His own replies add the detail the thread asked for — the elbows, moving in and out with the knees: 'sounds kinda stupid, but looked amazing.'

replies.author: @tomushy
replies.text: Damnit, I forgot the elbows! You wouldn't believe it, if I told you! :D

replies.author: @tomushy
replies.text: He moved his elbows and knees simultanously in- and outwards... sounds kinda stupid, but looked amazing.

cards.headline: Four words the thread built a ritual on: 'the leaving work track.'
cards.context: Its replies keep renaming it — the leaving-something-crappy track, the leaving-the-wife track.

replies.author: @Chimpfinga
replies.text: leaving the wife track in my case :)

replies.author: @glenseagles
replies.text: hahah. lets call it the leaving something crappy n pointless track.

cards.headline: Øya 2014: the live version half a million people dance to
cards.snippet: At Oslo's Øya Festival in 2014, Terje played the track live with the Olsens' dancers in strings of light; a fan upload of that performance has become the version's second home, watched more than 600,000 times. One listener: "Instead ofantidepressants people should be prescribed this video."
cards.context: Its own thread keeps prescribing the performance the same way — a depression-busting tune, a happy place, goosebumps on cue.

version.versionLabel: Todd Terje - Inspector Norse Best Live Version

cards.headline: Whateverest (2012): the film the video was cut from
cards.snippet: The track's official video is a four-minute excerpt from Borgli's short about Marius Solem Johansen, a small-town Norwegian who posted ecstatic solo dance videos online as 'Inspector Norse' — the excerpt keeps the film's joy and cuts loose its sadder whole.
cards.context: In the video's thread, the most-liked reading holds both halves at once: a sick father, a stuck village, home-cooked drugs — 'then music gives him an outlet.'
